title: Cisco Secure Endpoint Exploit Prevention Blocks
exclusions: Covers Windows connectors with Exploit Prevention enabled. macOS and Linux connectors do not report this event type.
evidence: Saved alert results with host, process, and detection, plus the patch or exclusion decision for each recurring process.

controlTest.positiveScenario: Pick an Exploit Prevention event from the Secure Endpoint console Events page in the last 30 days and run the search over the same window. It returns a row for that host with the same targeted process. In a lab, an exploit simulation approved by your security team against a protected process produces the same event.
controlTest.negativeScenario: Use the same application normally on the test host. No Exploit Prevention event is created and the search returns no row.

dataSources: `index=secure_endpoint sourcetype=cisco:se` from the Cisco Security Cloud (7404) Secure Endpoint input, which polls `GET /v1/events`. This search uses event type 1090519103 (Exploit Prevention). Each event carries `event_type`, `event_type_id`, `detection`, `severity`, `connector_guid`, `group_guids{}`, `computer.hostname`, `computer.user`, `computer.external_ip`, `computer.links.trajectory`, and for file events `file.file_name`, `file.file_path`, `file.disposition`, and `file.identity.sha256`.
app: Cisco Security Cloud (`CiscoSecurityCloud`, [Splunkbase 7404](https://splunkbase.splunk.com/app/7404)), Cisco Secure Endpoint input.
spl:
index=secure_endpoint sourcetype="cisco:se" event_type_id=1090519103
| eval host_name='computer.hostname', user='computer.user', sha256='file.identity.sha256', file_name='file.file_name', file_path='file.file_path', trajectory='computer.links.trajectory'
| stats count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(detection) as detections values(file_name) as processes values(file_path) as paths values(user) as users latest(trajectory) as trajectory by host_name
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| sort - count
description: Lists hosts where the Secure Endpoint Exploit Prevention engine blocked a memory-based exploit attempt against a protected process. Each row shows the detection, the targeted process and path, the users, and the trajectory link.
value: Exploit Prevention blocks attacks that work by injecting code into a legitimate process, which file scanning does not catch. A block means someone tried to exploit an application on that host; repeated blocks against one application point to a targeted attack or a vulnerable version that needs patching.
implementation: Enable Exploit Prevention in the Secure Endpoint policy for Windows connectors and collect events with the Cisco Security Cloud (7404) input into `index=secure_endpoint`. Schedule every 15 minutes and alert on every row.
visualization: Alert table: host_name, count, detections, processes, paths, users, firstTime, lastTime, trajectory. Supporting panel: exploit prevention events by targeted process over 30 days (bar chart).

knownFalsePositives:
1. **Application compatibility** — some legitimate software (older plugins, debuggers, DRM) behaves like an exploit and is blocked. These repeat on every launch of the same process on many hosts.

2. **Security tools** — other endpoint or monitoring agents that inject into processes can trigger blocks.

**Suppression:** add a process exclusion in the Secure Endpoint policy after review, and throttle per host and process for 4 hours.
detailedImplementation:
Prerequisites
• Cisco Security Cloud (`CiscoSecurityCloud`, Splunkbase 7404) on the search heads and on the heavy forwarder or Splunk Cloud Inputs Data Manager that runs its modular inputs.
• A Secure Endpoint API credential: in the Secure Endpoint console under Administration > API Credentials, create a read-only credential and record the client ID and API key, plus the API host for your region (for example `api.amp.cisco.com` for North America, `api.eu.amp.cisco.com` for Europe).
• Outbound HTTPS (TCP 443) from the input host to the API host.
• An index for Secure Endpoint data (this page uses `index=secure_endpoint`) and a role with `srchIndexesAllowed` on it for the SOC and endpoint teams.
• Exploit Prevention enabled in the Secure Endpoint policy (Policies > Modes and Engines > Exploit Prevention) for Windows connectors.

Step 1 — Configure data collection
• In Cisco Security Cloud open Application Setup, choose the Cisco Secure Endpoint card, and create an input with the API host, client ID, and API key. Set the index to `secure_endpoint`. The modular input polls `GET /v1/events` with a default interval of 300 seconds and writes `sourcetype=cisco:se`.
• Select the event types the input should collect. Collecting all types is simplest; if you limit them, include the event type IDs this search uses.
• In a distributed deployment run the input on one node only; the guide notes that the computers, compromises, and top-malware endpoints can produce duplicates otherwise.
• Check the events this search needs: run `index=secure_endpoint sourcetype=cisco:se event_type_id=1090519103 | stats count by detection` over 30 days.

Step 2 — Create the search and alert
```spl
index=secure_endpoint sourcetype="cisco:se" event_type_id=1090519103
| eval host_name='computer.hostname', user='computer.user', sha256='file.identity.sha256', file_name='file.file_name', file_path='file.file_path', trajectory='computer.links.trajectory'
| stats count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(detection) as detections values(file_name) as processes values(file_path) as paths values(user) as users latest(trajectory) as trajectory by host_name
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| sort - count
```

Understanding this SPL
• 1090519103 is Exploit Prevention; the event's `file` object describes the protected process that was targeted.
• `stats` by host keeps each targeted process and path, so a single host with several targeted applications stands out.

Step 3 — Validate
• Compare with the Secure Endpoint console Events page filtered to Exploit Prevention for the same time range: counts per host should match.
• Open the trajectory for one row and confirm the blocked process.
• Run `index=secure_endpoint sourcetype=cisco:se | timechart span=1h count by event_type` over 7 days; flat zero for all types for more than two intervals means the input stopped, not that the estate is clean.

Step 4 — Operationalize
• Schedule every 15 minutes over the last 20 minutes and throttle on `host_name` plus `processes` for 4 hours.
• Route to the SOC. If the same process is targeted on many hosts, check its version against current vendor advisories and patch.
• Review exclusions quarterly; remove any that are no longer needed.

Step 5 — Troubleshooting
• No cisco:se events and HTTP 401 in the input log: wrong client ID or API key, or the API host is for a different region from the organisation.
• Events arrive but `event_type_id` is missing: the events were indexed before JSON extraction applied; check `| fieldsummary` on one hour of data.
• Duplicate events with the same `id`: the input runs on more than one node, or the legacy AMP for Endpoints input (Splunkbase 3686) is still enabled. Keep one collector.
• No events for Windows hosts that should have them: Exploit Prevention is in audit mode or off in the policy for that group.
grandmaExplanation: Some attacks try to trick a normal program, like a web browser, into running bad code. The protection on the computer stopped one, and we tell the team which computer and program it was.
